TranScope: What the Software Hides About LLMs Training Data, the Hardware Reveals at Scale, and Accelerators Magnify

Joshua Kalyanapu, Darsh Asher, Kaushal Mhapsekar, Bita Aslrousta, Rushiraj Chaitanyakumar Sheth,
Maharshi Mukeshkumar Oza, Achyuta Kannan, and Samira Mirbagher Ajorpaz Affiliation:  North Carolina State University Affiliation:     HPCA \hpcayear Submission #\hpcasubmissionnumber Affiliation:  Confidential Draft
Do NOT Distribute!! Affiliation: 
Abstract

Membership is the root privacy primitive in machine learning: to date, no hardware-based out-of-distribution detection on black-box models has been demonstrated against constant-time, static neural networks with masked confidence.

This paper performs the first cycle-level examination of how large language models (LLMs) and vision transformers interact with various modern microarchitecture components, including integrated accelerators, as LLMs scale in size and answers the question of whether the data that a model was trained on affects its execution footprint even without any input-dependent branch, dynamic optimization, or early exit and in constant-time models.

The results confirm that the answer is yes and identify which modern hardware components, such as TLBs or on-core accelerators, reveal or amplify that effect. The results also answer whether the signal is informative enough to reliably classify the in-/vs/out-of-distribution property of membership.

To understand why, we perform a systematic root cause analysis and find that the transformer’s tokenization steps, which happen during training, alter the locality of the accesses the model makes to fetch the vocabulary token later during inference and, as a result, change the page table access patterns and TLB in a previously unknown data-dependent way, causing microarchitectural state to vary significantly based on whether or not the input was in the distribution of the transformer training data.

Building on the above observation, we introduce  TranScope: the first microarchitecture tool for detecting membership information with low cost, no need for a surrogate model, and significantly higher robustness, e.g., 0.6 AUC for PETAL (best previously reported) vs 0.9 AUC (ours). This reintroduces hardware as both an opportunity, e.g., a tool for checking copyright violation for the first time, and a new channel for inferring membership (MIA). TranScope achieves a surprisingly high out-of-distribution detection accuracy of 98% (1.5% FPR, 2.5% FNR) across large-scale models ranging from 4.4 million to 1.1 billion parameters.

I Introduction

Membership inference attacks on generative LLMs have proven to be not as straightforward as in classifier models. Duan et al. [1] shows how natural language lends itself to having a high degree of overlap between members and non-members, due to common phraseology appearing in natural language making members and non-members inherently similar. Meeus et al. [2] shows that most membership inference attacks on large-language models, particularly those benchmarking on the standard benchmark WikiMIA [3], rely on distributional shifts between members and nonmembers, reducing recent LLM membership inference attacks to out-of-distribution detection instead. The equivalence is intuitive: from a safety standpoint, we are much more concerned with whether a user John Doe’s social security number was used to train a model rather than whether the model was trained on the precise sentence ”John Doe’s social security number is X”. Therefore for language models, we treat out-of-distribution detection as equivalent to membership inference attacks as in prior work [4, 3, 5].

Traditional MIAs rely on confidence scores or logits. The standard defense is output discretization—rounding, quantizing, or binarizing confidence scores [6]. In production, logits are typically hidden, and many deployed MLaaS systems expose only labels. Figure 1 shows how output discretization has a devastating effect on traditional software-level MIAs, while TranScope is unaffected by them since TranScope does not use model outputs or confidences.

Recently, due to the proliferation of label-only model APIs research has shifted towards label-only membership inference attacks that do not rely on model internals or confidence scores. Instead, the model’s robustness to an input, or how much noise is required to change the model output given a specific input, is measured via random perturbations and the robustness is used as a proxy for confidence, and therefore membership. Choquette-Choo et al. [16] first presented a label-only attack on image classification models, finding comparable accuracy to confidence-based MIAs but required querying the expensive target model thousands of times. OSLO [12] overcame this limitation with a one-shot membership inference attack, using trained surrogate models to precisely apply the minimum amount of noise such that a nonmember will flip classification, but the methodology does not extend to large language models and requires training surrogate models. PETAL [5] presented the first label-only membership inference attack on language models, but requires running a comparable-in-size surrogate model which is expensive. To date, no label-only membership inference attack has been demonstrated that do not require expensive running of a surrogate model, function on language models, and do not require multiple queries to the model.

In concurrent work, Tong et al. [14] showed how the training dataset is encoded in the tokenizer itself, using the presence of distinctive and domain-specific tokens in publicly available tokenizers to infer in-distribution data. Like TranScope, Tong et al. leak membership through the tokenizer rather than the model itself, but unlike TranScope, Tong et al. leaks through the presence of specific tokens whereas TranScope leaks through the inter-token distance inducing membership-dependent read strides on the hardware. Since TranScope does not depend on the presence of specific tokens in the tokenizer vocabulary but rather token distance strides, Tong et al.’s mitigation of adaptively removing distinctive tokens from the vocabulary is ineffective against TranScope.

State-of-the-art membership inference attacks assume black-box access to AI models, where only a model’s outputs are visible and the internals of the models are invisible which mirrors membership inference attacks against remote model APIs. However, AI companies are shifting towards binarizing models to run locally to adhere to data residency policies that restrict inputting sensitive information to a cloud AI model. The model weights and parameters constitute a large amount of the value of an AI company, prompting the AI company to release models in binarized form instead of open-weight form. Therefore, we anticipate in the future that AI model releases will be closed-weight, and model users will have only black-box access despite the model running on a machine that the user has root access to. Examples of deployed local inference models with only black-box access include Apple Foundation Models [17], LLMWare’s Model HQ [18], Nvidia TensorRT-compiled models [19], Microsoft’s Phi Silica [20] and Aion Instruct [21], and Adobe Firefly [22]. Downloadable, closed-weight models that do not provide confidence scores disable confidence-based membership inference attacks and out-of-distribution detection force us to rely on expensive label-only membership inference attacks which are infeasible on low-power user hardware.

The trend is clear - industry is moving towards binarized models, mitigating all white-box and confidence-score-based membership inference attacks and necessitating label-only attacks. Existing label-only attacks are expensive, requiring thousands of queries to a model, training a surrogate model, or running a surrogate model. Table I positions TranScope within the literature, showing it as the first attack to not use confidence scores or outputs, not require an adaptive neural network, functions on language models, bypasses all existing MIA mitigations, does not require training or querying an expensive surrogate model, and only requires querying the target model once making it suitable for real-time deployment.

Limitations of prior hardware-assisted MIAs. GateBleed (MICRO 2025) [13] was the first to exploit hardware to bypass output-discretization defenses, achieving 81% accuracy via Intel AMX power-gating timing. However, GateBleed rests on a structural assumption that disqualifies it from the majority of modern systems: the target model must contain an entropy-dependent branch that causes different computation for member versus nonmember inputs. Adaptive networks such as BranchyNet [23] and Mixture-of-Experts [24] satisfy this condition, but dominant modern models—LLaMA [25], BERT [26], GPT, Vision Transformers—execute static forward passes, providing no input-dependent branch for GateBleed to exploit. Our measurements confirm that end-to-end inference time for GPT and BERT is statistically indistinguishable between member and nonmember samples to within 1.2% across all model sizes and microarchitectures—the timing or usage signal on which GateBleed and all prior hardware-based membership inference attacks depend simply does not exist in modern models. Furthermore, GateBleed also requires an unpatched Intel AMX [27], present only on Sapphire Rapids through Granite Rapids CPUs, producing no signal on earlier microarchitectures or non-Intel microarchitectures. GhostTrace [15] presents a GPU performance-counter based membership inference attack on CNNs and ViT, but achieves lower accuracy than  TranScope due to the relatively few performance counters exposed by GPUs as compared to CPUs.

Prior works EVAX [28], PerSpectron [29], and RHMD [30] demonstrated that malicious computation from transient-execution attacks such as Spectre [31, 32], Meltdown [33], FallOut [34], and LVI [35] leaves microarchitectural footprints detectable through hardware performance monitoring. Our work flips this premise. Instead of detecting microarchitectural side channels we use microarchitectural footprints to build a lightweight, fast detector for copyright abuse detection and leak properties of training data of production AI models including GPT [36], BERT [26], and Vision Transformers [37]— modern transformer architectures; not only with significantly higher robustness than software methods [14] but also bypassing all confidence masking defenses [6].

This paper demonstrates that the microarchitectural landscape can leak training-data provenance: whether a transformer or CNN has been shaped by a specific sample or a copyright-relevant stylistic property. Privacy-critical training data reshapes the internal mechanics of modern models—via embeddings, and locality—into differences that are not merely statistically detectable, but often visibly observable in standard microarchitectural counters (page-table walks, cache demand misses, prefetch-hit behavior, pipeline clears). Crucially, these leaks persist even when end-to-end timing changes by less than 1.2%, bypassing constant-time defenses entirely—undermining the intuition that “if the same high-level inference code runs, the hardware footprint should be the same.” We establish the root cause as a tokenizer-induced spatial-locality gap: training changes which embedding rows are hot, and that locality difference propagates into TLB walk counts, off-core memory traffic, and reservation-station pressure while remaining invisible to timing.

Even more critically, we show that microarchitectural training-data provenance leakage grows with model size, reflecting the effect of larger model sizes memorizing more of the training set [38]. Figure 2 illustrates this point - a basic confidence-threshold membership inference attack jumps from 70% accuracy to 96% accuracy when the model surpasses 100M parameters. Our  TranScope attacks on BERT and Pythia exhibit similar behavior.

Figure 3 additionally shows how power-consumption disparity between members and nonmembers, one statistic utilized by TranScope, grows with model size further highlighting the growing AI privacy threat with increasing model size. As AI models scale in size, TranScope is not going away but will only become stronger.

Unlike traditional microarchitectural side channels such as Spectre [39], Meltdown [33]—which leak stored information (cryptographic keys, pointers, model weights)—TranScope targets information not stored as bytes on the machine: training-set membership, a latent property of the learned model previously not believed to be inferrable from hardware alone.

TranScope is neither a TLBleed [7] nor a traditional cache attack which encode victim memory in the TLB and cache for later extraction by an attacker — while TranScope does use the TLB and cache, TranScope targets training-set membership, a property stored nowhere in victim memory. Similar to Cache Telepathy [9] which used known cache attacks to attack AI models, TranScope also attacks AI models; however, while Cache Telepathy targets model architecture and hyperparameters, TranScope targets training-set membership. This paper contains many unexpected results that are fundamental to hardware security in protecting user data used for training these models.

Out-of-Distribution Detection and Membership Inference Attacks. Out-of-distribution detection (OOD) asks whether a specific record is within the training-set distribution of a model; informally, whether the input is similar to the data the model was trained on. Out-of-distribution detection was first described by Hendrycks et al. in 2016 [40], using model outputs due to models being overconfidently incorrect on inputs not drawn from its training distribution, leading to AI safety issues described by Amodei et al. [41] which have manifested in the real world. In 2018, a pedestrian was killed by a self-driving Uber due to the software not recognizing the possibility of jaywalking pedestrians [42]. In 2016, a driver was killed when colliding with a tractor-trailer while using Tesla Autopilot, which failed to identify the tractor trailer crossing into the driver’s lane and prompt for human intervention [43]. Thus, the inability of a model to identify inputs unlike its training set to flag a human for manual intervention can yield disastrous results.

Related to out-of-distribution detection are membership inference attacks (MIAs), which ask whether a specific, in-distribution input was in the training set [6, 8]. Membership is a sensitive and legally actionable fact—determining whether a cancer scan, private message, or copyrighted manuscript was used for training can establish violations of medical privacy, confidentiality agreements, or copyright. Recent headlines make this concrete: Getty Images sued Stability AI for training on copyrighted images [44]; LinkedIn was accused of training on private messages; Apple was sued for allegedly using pirated books to train AI models [45]. Foundational MIA work [6, 8] has accumulated thousands of citations because membership is the root privacy primitive: a model that behaves differently on training-set members versus non-members enables escalation to attribute inference and, in the worst case, model inversion.

TranScope removes both constraints simultaneously while achieving over 95% membership inference accuracy in most cases. By observing 290+ hardware performance counters rather than a single timing scalar, it detects membership leakage in static, branchless, production transformer networks—BERT [26], ViT [46], GPT [36], and Pythia [47]—on Intel Sapphire Rapids, without requiring any specialized accelerator or adaptive computation. We demonstrate that 27+ counter events exhibit statistically significant member-versus-nonmember divergence when timing is constant and every prior defense and attack is blind.

Our 290+ event traces reveal that LLMs and vision transformers do not stress the processor uniformly: training familiarity, input entropy, and model scale reshape branch behavior, front-end delivery, TLB activity, cache locality, reservation-station occupancy, execution-port pressure, power, and latency across the full pipeline. Each counter disparity is simultaneously a leakage signal and a design signal, motivating embedding-aware TLB partitioning, large-page-backed embedding tables, and branchless pooling primitives.

Legal cases involving copyrighted data in AI training have proliferated: Thomson Reuters v. Ross [48], Doe v. GitHub [49], Andersen v. Stability AI [50], Getty Images v. Stability AI [44], Concord Music v. Anthropic [51], UMG v. Suno [52], NYT v. OpenAI [53], Bartz v. Anthropic [54], and Kadrey v. Meta [55]. We validate TranScope on the same corpus at the center of the New York Times Co. v. OpenAI. litigation, using real copyrighted NYT articles—not synthetic benchmarks—to demonstrate that pre-2019 (potential member) and post-2019 (definite non-member) articles separate in counter space despite identical software execution.

Contributions. This paper makes the following contributions:

  • •

    We investigate the potential of microarchitectural MIA on static, branchless production transformer, bypassing constant-time defenses. We show that 15 Intel counter events and power consumption expose training-set membership in BERT, ViT, GPT, and LLaMA yielding AUC 0.995, 99.8% accuracy, TPR 100%, FPR 0.5% on a realistic threat model available to common users of these popular models, rendering confidence masking and constant-time padding ineffective.

  • •

    We trace the causal chain from training corpus vocabulary statistics through token-ID proximity and embedding-row spatial locality to cache/TLB residency and observable counter divergence and show the tokenizer effect on embedding locality affecting TLB is the root cause for LLM membership leakage.

  • •

    We show how  TranScope bypasses software-level confidence masking and constant time padding for membership inference defenses due to TranScope’s lack of reliance on model outputs, confidences, and end-to-end execution time. As a first line-of-defense for mitigating  TranScope, we recommend restricting tokenizer training during fine-tuning. Further defenses include smoothing embedding table accesses by sorting token IDs, making the spatial footprint of familiar and novel inputs more similar. We also introduce the concept of constant-footprint execution, where an AI inference system equalizes not only end-to-end runtime but other microarchitectural statistics like TLB accesses, execution port utilization, and per-inference energy consumption.

Responsible Disclosure. We disclosed TranScope to Intel in July 2026. Intel reproduced our results and confirmed our findings.

Paper organization. Section II enumerates the legal and malicious threat models under which we operate. Section III details the  TranScope attack. Section IV describes our experimental environment, including hardware, models, and datasets. Section V details the microarchitectural insights we glean to improve model execution from observing the performance counters generated by  TranScope. Section VI discusses related work, and Section VII concludes.

II Threat Model

We consider a legal threat model where  TranScope imposes no requirements on the victim: the attacker does not need to synchronise with, observe, or force the victim to repeat queries. In fact, there is no victim at all—the attacker, or legal auditor, is the user.

Legal threat model (privileged auditor).

The attacker downloads a publicly-available model and runs it on hardware they own and control. This is not a hypothetical scenario; it is the default operating mode of every user who interacts with a publicly released language model today. Models such as GPT [36], LLaMA [25], and BERT [26] are distributed as open weights executable on any commodity CPU without specialized drivers, CUDA installation, or minimum VRAM. Furthermore, industry is shifting towards shipping binarized, closed-weight models runnable on commodity hardware, such as Apple Foundation Models [17], Microsoft Aion Instruct [21], and Adobe Firefly [22], allowing only black-box model accesses even when running on an attacker-controlled machine. The attacker downloads the model, inputs the disputed artifact to it, and reads the hardware counters on their own machine. There is no co-location problem, no hypervisor to evade, no victim with which to synchronize, and no need for the model owner to cooperate or be aware that the measurement is taking place. The attacker controls the entire measurement stack: the hardware, the OS, the inference runtime, and the input.

This is the most realistic attacker model in the side-channel literature, because it requires zero capabilities beyond those already available to every user who downloads a publicly-released model. The goal is to build a hardware footprint that separates data matching the model’s training distribution from data that does not, producing corroborating evidence for legal proceedings.

The CPU is the strongest measurement platform for this purpose: Intel Sapphire Rapids exposes 263 publicly documented core performance monitoring events spanning branch prediction, front-end delivery, TLB activity, cache hierarchy, scheduler pressure, execution-port utilization, retirement, and software-prefetch behavior—orders of magnitude more signal than GPU performance counters.

Auditor and expert-witness models.

In forensic settings, a court-appointed or party-retained auditor receives the artifact(s) under investigation, control corpora, and controlled model access. The deliverable is a reproducible evidence bundle satisfying Federal Rule of Evidence 702 and the Daubert standard [56]. The TranScope protocol anticipates both plaintiff- and defendant-assisted audits.

Empirical validation on real copyrighted articles.

We apply TranScope to GPT on real New York Times article snippets—copyrighted content from the NYT API, not synthetic benchmarks. We separate articles by GPT’s disclosed training cutoff: pre-October 2019 (candidate members) versus post-2019 (definite non-members). The results reveal statistically significant hardware footprint differences that appear as a monotonic trend over publication date—precisely the signal a coarse aggregate histogram would obscure.

III TranScope

III-A Overview

A model trained on a corpus 𝒟\mathcal{D} implicitly optimizes its hardware access pattern for inputs drawn from 𝒟\mathcal{D}. Familiar inputs access a compact, hot region of the embedding table, stressing the TLB and caches in predictable ways. On the other hand, novel inputs scatter accesses across the embedding table, accessing a larger swath of the embedding table resulting in more TLB and cache misses. These effects are invisible at the level of the Python forward pass—the same operators execute in the same order—yet are measurable via hardware performance counters.

TranScope measures the distributional distance between an inference input and the model’s training distribution, as reflected in hardware telemetry. This is why TranScope is framed around in-distribution/out-of-distribution rather than member/nonmember: it is a statistical characterization of whether the input has the same “spirit” as the training corpus.

Provenance witness.

We define a provenance witness as a hardware-visible or model-internal signal whose behavior is statistically consistent with prior exposure to a disputed artifact, or to a narrowly defined artifact class, and which can therefore serve as corroborating evidence regarding the artifact’s origin or training influence. No single witness settles a case in isolation; when multiple witnesses shift coherently—TLB activity, token locality, and power all moving in the same direction—they collectively form a strong provenance argument.

III-B Root Cause: Tokenizer-Induced Embedding Locality

Core claim.

The counter divergence between familiar and unfamiliar inputs is not noise across independent hardware events. It is the projection of a single microarchitectural mechanism with a traceable causal chain:

training-corpus familiarity →\;\rightarrow\; token-ID proximity →\;\rightarrow\; embedding-row locality →\;\rightarrow\; cache/TLB residency →\;\rightarrow\; counter divergence.

We make this concrete with an example shown below and in Figure 4. Suppose we have a large language model whose training cutoff was 2020. Then, if the model was trained on news articles around the cutoff time it would have encountered many headlines relating to COVID-19 (early 2020) but it would not have encountered any headlines relating to the Russo-Ukrainian war (early 2022).

Two articles, two memory landscapes.

Consider an example headline from March 2020: “COVID-19 spreads in Wuhan as cases rise; China reports new virus infections.” When the model’s tokenizer processes this sentence, it maps each word to an integer ID that serves as a row index into the model’s embedding table. Because words like “China,” “virus,” and “spread” appeared millions of times in the model’s training corpus, the tokenizer learned to assign them small, numerically nearby IDs: for example, China (2859), virus (3142), spread (4293). These IDs would cluster in a narrow band in the vocabulary.

Now consider an example headline from February 2022: “Russia invades Ukraine with full-scale attack, shelling near Kyiv.” The words “Kyiv,” “invasion,” and “shelling” would be rare or absent in the model’s training data. The tokenizer would assign them large, widely spaced IDs, for example: Kyiv (27631), invasion (18204), shelling (14208). These IDs scatter across a vast range of the vocabulary.

From IDs to memory addresses.

Each token ID rtr_{t} indexes a row in the embedding table at address addr​(rt)=BASE+rt⋅dmodel⋅sizeof(float)\texttt{addr}(r_{t})=\texttt{BASE}+r_{t}\cdot d_{\text{model}}\cdot\texttt{sizeof(float)}. For BERT-base (dmodel=768d_{\text{model}}=768, fp32), each row occupies 768×4=3,072768\times 4=3{,}072 bytes—nearly filling a single 4 KB memory page. The physical distance the processor must jump between successive token lookups is proportional to the difference in their IDs. For the member pair China →\to virus, the stride is 283×3,072≈0.83283\times 3{,}072\approx 0.83 MB—a short hop within a few neighbouring memory pages. For the non-member pair Kyiv →\to invasion, the stride is 9,427×3,072≈28.99{,}427\times 3{,}072\approx 28.9 MB—a 35×\times larger jump that leaps across thousands of pages the processor has never seen in this inference.

What the hardware sees.

The CPU maintains a translation lookaside buffer (TLB) that caches recent virtual-to-physical page mappings. When successive embedding lookups land on nearby pages, the TLB already holds the translation: the access is a fast hit, resolved in a few cycles. When lookups scatter across distant pages, each new page forces a page-table walk—the processor must traverse four levels of the page-table hierarchy in memory, costing roughly 200 cycles per walk.

Figure 5 makes this concrete. In this experiment, we created a dataset consisting of token sequences of length 512, beginning as entirely random sequences and setting an increasing amount of tokens within the sequence to 0 until the last item in the dataset, an all-zero token sequence. We run the dataset through all canonical BERT sizes, finding that tiny, mini, small, medium, and base exhibit a clear trend of increasing page table walks for increasing amount of nonzero tokens. Large stays flat at a constant number of page table walks, we attribute this to the large size of the model drowning out the contribution of the embedding table accesses. However, in Section IV we find that many performance counter observations can be combined in aggregate to determine out-of-distribution from in-distribution data at high accuracy, even for large models.

For the candidate member article, the clustered token IDs produce a compact memory footprint. The embedding rows land on ≤70\leq\!70 distinct pages, and most of those pages stay TLB-resident throughout inference. The processor follows the fast path: TLB hit, L1/L2 cache hit, no page-table walk.

For the non-member article, the scattered IDs spray accesses across many different pages. The TLB overflows, and each new page triggers the slow path: TLB miss, second-level TLB miss, last-level cache miss, page-table walk, and finally a DRAM fetch.

The model executes an identical sequence of neural-network operations in the same number of clock cycles for both articles—the difference in page-table walks is too small (20 walks out of 52 million cycles) to surface in end-to-end timing, yet the hardware counters that track TLB misses, off-core memory traffic, and reservation-station pressure tell different stories. This is the signal TranScope reads and why constant-time padding provides no defense.

Statistical confirmation.

Figure 6 confirms the successive token-distance gap across all five BERT model sizes: the in-distribution CDF rises sharply at small token distances, while the out-of-distribution CDF is consistently heavier-tailed.

Key insight.

The processor is not reacting to input data semantics; it is reacting to the geometry of embedding memory accesses induced by the tokenizer. All measured counters—fewer page-table walk completions for members, fewer off-core demand reads for members, more reservation-station stalls for members (because loads retire faster and the back-end fills up)—are correlated projections of this single root cause. The difference is consistent across models, observable across hundreds of counter events, and invisible in end-to-end timing.

III-C Algorithm

TranScope is organized around four design principles: (P1) non-invasive measurement (the model is treated as a fixed artifact); (P2) multi-witness evidence (263 counters organized across seven subsystems form a jury, not a single gadget); (P3) controlled execution (core placement, SMT, frequency, prefetcher state, and input normalization form a disclosed configuration manifest); (P4) method separated from conclusion (output is corroborating evidence, not a binary legal verdict).

The system proceeds in five stages: (1) artifact conditioning—defining the provenance question and constructing familiar/novel reference sets; (2) controlled execution harness—applying hardware configuration controls; (3) target-model inference—executing on both reference sets and the disputed artifact; (4) multi-witness footprint collection—recording counter telemetry, power, latency, and token locality; (5) analysis and evidence generation—computing effect sizes, subsystem grouping, and emitting an auditable report.

III-D Step-by-Step Attack Walkthrough: Example BERT

We provide an example of the TranScope attack on the 110.1 M-parameter BERT-base model trained for sentiment classification on 1,000 IMDB reviews [57].

Step 1: Reference set construction.

The familiar set 𝒳F\mathcal{X}_{F} consists of 1,000 IMDB reviews from the training split. The novel set 𝒳N\mathcal{X}_{N} consists of 1,000 sequences of uniformly sampled token IDs from the BERT vocabulary, matched in length.

Step 2: Execution and counter collection.

Each input is tokenized and padded to 512 tokens. The model executes on a single core pinned via taskset, SMT disabled, TurboBoost enabled, prefetchers at factory defaults. We collect all available performance counters on the system using PAPI [60], plus RAPL energy.

Step 3: Key observation.

Figure 7 shows the result. End-to-end latency is statistically identical (∼52{\sim}52 M cycles), yet page-table walk completions are elevated by ∼20{\sim}20 walks for out-of-distribution inputs—consistent with the embedding-table locality mechanism.

Step 4: MCF score computation.

For each witness w∈𝒲w\in\mathcal{W}, compute the zz-score of the disputed artifact relative to the familiar and novel reference distributions. Aggregate across witnesses to produce a subsystem-level summary and overall MCF score.

Step 5: Evidence report.

The final report includes per-counter effect sizes with 95% bootstrap CIs, a subsystem-level heatmap, the MCF score with estimated false-positive rate, and the full configuration manifest.

IV Evaluation

IV-A Experimental Methodology

Hardware configuration.

All experiments run on a single isolated core pinned via core affinity, with isolcpus removing the core from the OS scheduler. All experiments run with TurboBoost enabled (800 MHz–4.1 GHz). SMT is disabled in all primary experiments. Counter access requires perf_event_paranoid = −-1 (CAP_PERFMON on Linux 5.8+). Experiments marked IPEX use Intel Extensions for Pytorch, a Pytorch backend that makes use of Intel-specific features like AMX, rather than the default Pytorch CPU backend.

Models.

We study three model architecture families spanning recent transformers: BERT (4.4 M, 11.3 M, 29.1 M, 41.7 M, 110.1 M parameters) fine-tuned for sentiment classification on the Large Movie Review Dataset [57]; ViT (22 M, 86 M, 307 M parameters) trained on ImageNet [59] for image classification, and Pythia (70M, 160M, 410M, 1B, 1.4B, 2.8B parameters), a language model mimicking LLaMA [25] but with disclosed training data [47].

Datasets.

Each model is paired with a corpus designed to isolate training-exposure effects as seen in Table II: (i) controlled-entropy images (ViT): CIFAR samples (ID) interpolated with uniform entropy (OOD), decoupling input entropy from content semantics; (ii) semantically-structured vs. random tokens (BERT-Random): 1,000 IMDB reviews (in-distribution) vs. 1,000 uniformly sampled random token sequences (out-of-distribution); (iii) Tokens from two different semantic contexts (BERT-NIH, BERT-Enron): 1,000 NIH Exporter samples (in-distribution) vs. 1,000 Enron Emails (out-of-distribution), and vice versa (iv) Pre/post-training-cutoff corpus (NYT): copyrighted articles before GPT’s training cutoff (in-distribution) vs. post-cutoff (out-of-distribution). All inputs are matched in length and size, ensuring that the same amount of work executes for each sample; therefore, any performance counter differences we find are due to how the model reacts to the input.

IV-B Emergent Counter Rankings

We define a counter as emergent if it exhibits medium-to-high effect size (d≥0.5d\geq 0.5, p≤0.15p\leq 0.15) in the member-vs.-nonmember comparison. By convention, d≥0.5d\geq 0.5 is medium, d≥0.8d\geq 0.8 is large, and d≥1.5d\geq 1.5 is exceptional.

Figure 8 ranks 13 emergent counters for BERT-tiny (4.4 M) on the Haswell microarchitecture. Counters relating to page-table walks exhibit emergent behavior and achieve the strongest separation between member and nonmember (d=0.75d=0.75—0.820.82). The rest of the emergent counters are related to cache misses, like L1D cache replacement, ROB stalls, offcore data reads, L2 misses, and cycles handling L1 misses. Figure 9 shows four emergent counters for Vision Transformers — scalar FP instructions, double-precision FP instructions, taken branches, and software prefetches. Notably in the ViT and BERT cases, total cycle count and end-to-end timing are not emergent, confirming that the leakage bypasses constant-time defenses.

Figure 10 ranks the top 15 emergent counters for ViT-base (86 M) on Sapphire Rapids. Floating-point microcode assists ASSISTS.FP dominates at d=2.52d=2.52—the largest effect size across all model–architecture pairs in this study and the largest hardware-based membership effect size reported to date.

IV-C Power Side-Channel

Per-inference socket power (Intel RAPL, SGX enabled) reveals a third independent leakage channel orthogonal to both performance counters and timing. Figure 3 shows power normalised to the BERT-tiny member baseline. The member/non-member gap grows monotonically from +2.6%+2.6\% at BERT-mini to +4.5%+4.5\% at BERT-base, tracking model parameter count. End-to-end wall-clock time is flat to within 1.2% across all sizes, confirming that timing defenses fail—yet RAPL power provides a complementary and growing signal.

IV-D BERT Member/Nonmember Classifier Study

We collected the performance counter, energy, and power statistics for all BERT sizes on Sapphire Rapids across 100 samples of the IMDB dataset and 100 samples of verified non members of the same size which we generated with 10 repeats per sample and stacked the resulting statistics into a dataset of 2000 samples each with 1,596 features. We trained a 4-layer multilayer perceptron classifier on the the resultant data using an 80/20 train/test split, with the layers having 512, 128, 32, and one neuron, respectively. We trained for 10 epochs with a dropout of 0.4 in the first 2 layers. Table III contains our results. In most cases, we achieved an accuracy of over 90% in determining IMDB samples vs random sequences using only performance counters, regardless of model size.

Similarly, we repeated the Structured v Random experiment with BERT running on Intel Extensions for Pytorch (IPEX), a backend using Intel AMX and Intel AVX-512-VNNI kernels representing modern accelerator hardware. Interestingly, we see a clear monotonic increase in AUC and accuracy for increasing model size when using the IPEX backend, implying the use of modern accelerator hardware makes TranScope more effective at larger model sizes.

Finally, we repeat the methodology except using the Enron v NIH and NIH v Enron datasets to see if TranScope can distinguish between two nonuniform distributions. We find that despite both in-distribution and out-of-distribution texts being valid sentences, TranScope is still easily able to separate member and non-member with 98% accuracy.

As Figure 11 shows, both the false-positive and false-negative rates drop to near zero once the model exceeds ∼30{\sim}30 M parameters for BERT and ∼70{\sim}70 M for Pythia, confirming that the attack signal strengthens with capacity.

IV-E New York Times Articles Study

We collected the performance counter and timing statistics of running GPT on New York Times articles from 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, and 2023. GPT’s training cutoff was November 2019; hence, the article from 2019 is a possible member, or at least in-distribution, to GPT’s training set whereas the articles from 2020-2023 can not be. Figure 12 shows the result of this study, finding that the 2019 article exhibits 56% fewer off-core demand reads over the 2020-2023 articles and 12% fewer DTLB load misses, all while remaining within 1% of runtime bypassing constant-time defenses. Therefore, GPT is more familiar with the 2019 article than the other articles, fitting what we know about the training date cutoff.

V Microarchitectural Insights and Redesign Guidance

This paper does more than introduce a new family of side channels. Its deeper contribution is architectural: it provides one of the first detailed CPU-side characterisations of how production CNNs, LLMs, and vision transformers stress the microarchitecture, how that stress changes with input familiarity, and how it evolves as model size scales. Across more than 290 hardware performance counters, along with latency, energy, and power, we show that training influence does not remain confined to model outputs—it reshapes the execution footprint of the processor itself. Production transformers do not stress the processor uniformly: training predictability and model scale reshape branch behavior, front-end delivery, TLB activity, cache locality, reservation-station occupancy, execution-port pressure, power, and latency across the full microarchitecture pipeline.

These results therefore matter not only to privacy and security researchers, but also to performance architects and hardware designers, because each counter disparity is simultaneously a leakage signal and a clue about where modern AI workloads stress, underutilise, or destabilise the machine.

Translation structures.

Page-table walk completions for 2 MB/4 MB pages increase with BERT model size and separate familiar from novel inputs across all five parameter points. Transformer embedding-table access patterns stress the page-table walker far more than prior workloads—300+ walk completions per inference, each costing hundreds of cycles [61] This motivates embedding-aware TLB partitioning, large-page-backed embedding tables, and speculative page-walk prefetch tuned to gather/scatter access patterns.

Speculation recovery.

Pipeline clears (d≈0.84d\approx 0.84) and pipeline recovery cycles (d≈0.73d\approx 0.73) differ between familiar and novel inputs even when wall-clock time does not—further evidence that the leakage operates below the timing floor and bypasses constant-time defenses. Future CPUs targeting LLM inference could benefit from “ML-phase” hints that adapt branch-predictor confidence thresholds for out-of-distribution inputs.

Cache hierarchy and prefetch.

Embedding-table scatter drives L3 miss counts and off-core demand reads for novel inputs; familiar inputs enjoy greater cache residency because the model has been conditioned to their token distribution. Prefetcher designs that recognize embedding-table stride signatures could reduce both miss rates and the locality-driven leakage that TranScope exploits.

Scheduler pressure.

Reservation-station empty cycles and store-buffer stalls vary with both model size and input familiarity, revealing phases where speculative work and memory-latency hiding interact with novelty-driven traffic.

Power and energy.

Per-inference power differs between familiar and novel inputs even when latency does not, constituting a leakage channel orthogonal to timing [62] as shown in Figure 3. Increasing training-set coverage reduces average inference energy; “training coverage” becomes a new axis in energy modeling of production LLM deployments.

VI Related Work

Software-based membership inference.

The foundational MIA by Shokri et al. [6] used shadow models to infer membership from classification outputs. LiRA [8] improved attack power through likelihood-ratio tests. Label-only attacks [16] showed that differential privacy [63] is the only effective defense. Subsequent work extended MIAs to recommender systems [64], federated learning [65], in-context learning [66], vision-language models [67], and LLMs [68]. All prior works require model outputs, confidence scores, running an expensive surrogate model, or multiple inferences; TranScope is the first cheap, one-shot out-of-distribution detector that does not require any model output or surrogate model.

Hardware-assisted privacy attacks.

GateBleed [13] exploits Intel AMX power-gating timing for MIA on adaptive networks. FeatureBleed [69] infers private attributes from sparsity-optimized accelerators. Timing-channel attacks [10] target adaptive neural networks with observable latency variation. TranScope is the first to demonstrate membership leakage on static, branchless, production networks where timing is constant and all prior hardware-assisted attacks fail.

Property inference.

Property inference attacks [70] determine undisclosed properties of training data. Extensions cover GANs [71], CNNs [72], graph neural networks [73], and federated learning [74]. TranScope subsumes property inference as a special case: when the “property” is membership in a temporal slice of a publisher’s archive, our hardware footprint provides direct evidence.

Microarchitectural side channels.

Prior work establishes that timing channels persist on formally verified kernels [75] and surveys the attack surface exhaustively [76]. Our finding that 15+ counter events discriminate training members from nonmembers while timing remains flat adds a new entry to that taxonomy: a software-optimization-mediated counter channel that operates below the timing floor. Our 290+ event trace dataset enables the community to compute formal channel-capacity bounds for each leaking event across three model families and two microarchitectures.

Microarchitectural characterization of AI workloads.

While this paper introduces a new series of side-channel techniques, its broader contribution is to expose the microarchitectural anatomy of modern AI execution on CPUs. Prior CPU characterization studies have focused on traditional server workloads; no prior work has systematically profiled how training familiarity, input entropy, and model scale reshape the full microarchitecture pipeline—from branch prediction through TLB activity and cache locality to execution-port utilization and power. This paper is therefore not only a security result; it is also a microarchitectural characterization study of production AI workloads, with direct implications for future processor optimization and hardware design. Our traces show that transformer embedding lookups generate 300+ page-table walk completions per inference on Sapphire Rapids, each costing hundreds of cycles—a bottleneck invisible to prior workload characterization and one that motivates embedding-aware TLB partitioning and large-page-backed embedding table layouts.

VII Conclusion

Membership inference is the root of privacy in modern AI. This paper establishes that hardware detectors can bypass state-of-the-art software defenses in constant time models, and alarmingly, these hardware-level leakage signals amplify as models—such as LLMs, Vision Transformers, and CNNs—scale and as new accelerators gets integrated in CPUS. Consequently, user privacy is fundamentally vulnerable at the hardware level. As AI becomes ubiquitous across all computing domains, and hardware accelerators becoming more integrated, relying solely on software defenses is no longer sufficient. TranScope takes the first step in analyzing how these privacy-compromising hardware signals manifest as we relentlessly scale and deploy these models or integrate aggressive on core acceleration for AI.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
